summary: Describes a protocol that provides lossless compression for IP datagrams, so packets can be made smaller before being sent.

plainLanguage.summary: It squishes packages so they fit better, then unsquishes them at the other end.

questions: how does ip payload compression work
what is a compression parameter index
subtitle: How to shrink IP packet payloads before sending, and how two nodes agree to do it.

tldr.problem: Slow or congested links waste capacity on bulky IP datagrams, and once a datagram is encrypted it looks random, so compression at lower layers no longer helps.
tldr.mechanism: IPComp compresses each IP payload on its own, inserts a 4-byte IPComp header, and sets the IP protocol or next header value to 108. Two nodes first set up an IPComp Association, usually through IKE.
tldr.outcome: Compression happens before encryption and fragmentation, and a datagram that would not shrink is sent unchanged. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2393 and mostly clarifies how IKE negotiates the association.

today: RFC 3173 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2393, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Compress IP Payloads
sections.content:
IP payload compression (IPComp) reduces the size of IP datagrams. It improves communication between a pair of nodes (hosts or gateways) when they have enough computing power, either CPU capacity or a compression coprocessor, and the link between them is slow or congested.

It matters most when encryption is in use. Encrypting a datagram makes its data random in nature, so compression at lower layers, such as the PPP Compression Control Protocol in RFC 1962, becomes ineffective. If both compression and encryption are needed, compression must be applied before encryption.

The RFC defines the protocol, the packet structure, the IPComp Association (IPCA) and several ways to negotiate that association. The compression algorithms themselves are left to other documents.
sections.plainLanguage: Locked boxes cannot be squished, so you must squish your stuff first and lock the box afterwards. IPComp does the squishing step.

sections.title: The Compression Process
sections.content:
Compression must be lossless: after a datagram is compressed and decompressed it must be identical to the original. Each datagram is handled by itself, with no relation to other datagrams, because datagrams may arrive out of order or not at all. Inbound processing must accept both compressed and non-compressed datagrams.

Order of operations matters. On the way out, compression MUST come before any IP security processing such as encryption and authentication, and before any fragmentation. In IPv6 it MUST also come before a Hop-by-Hop Options header or a Routing Header is added, because those carry information that nodes along the path may need to read. On the way in, decompression MUST happen after reassembly and after authentication and decryption are done.

The compressed part is one contiguous run of octets that ends at the last octet of the IP payload. In IPv4 it starts right after the IP header, and no part of the IP header or its options is compressed. With tunnel mode encapsulation in IPsec, the inner IP header counts as payload and is compressed. In IPv6, IPComp MUST NOT apply to hop-by-hop, routing and fragmentation extension headers. The compressed size must be a whole number of octets.
sections.plainLanguage: You squish only the contents of the envelope, never the address on the front. And you squish before you lock and before you cut things into pieces.

sections.title: The Non-Expansion Policy
sections.content:
If the compressed payload plus the IPComp header is not smaller than the original payload, the datagram MUST be sent in its original form, and no IPComp header is added. This saves decompression work and avoids fragmentation when an expanded datagram would be larger than the MTU.

Two further hints are given. Small datagrams are likely to expand, so a numeric threshold should be applied and smaller datagrams sent without trying compression; the threshold is implementation dependent. Payloads that were already compressed, for example by an upper layer or an offline utility, tend not to shrink further, so an adaptive algorithm should skip compression for some datagrams after repeated failures and restart normal processing after one succeeds. The details of that algorithm are also implementation dependent.

The compression algorithm MAY also test compressibility periodically, similar to V.42 bis, and SHOULD stop processing the data once it detects the data is non-compressible.
sections.plainLanguage: If squishing does not make the bag smaller, do not bother. Send it as it was, and do not waste time trying on tiny or already-squished things.

sections.title: The IPComp Header and IP Header Changes
sections.content:
A compressed datagram is built by changing the IP header and inserting a four-octet IPComp header right before the compressed payload. In IPv4 the Total Length covers the IP header, the IPComp header and the compressed payload, the Protocol field is set to 108 (IPComp Datagram), and the header checksum is recomputed. In IPv6 the Payload Length is the length of the compressed IP payload and the Next Header field is set to 108. All other fields are kept unchanged.

The IPComp header holds three fields. Next Header (8 bits) stores the original IPv4 Protocol or IPv6 Next Header value. Flags (8 bits) is reserved: it MUST be set to zero and MUST be ignored by the receiver. The 16-bit Compression Parameter Index (CPI) identifies the algorithm and is stored in network order.

In IPv6 the IPComp header is placed using the same rules as the IPv6 Fragment Header. If a packet has both, the Fragment Header MUST come first.
sections.plainLanguage: The IPComp header is a small sticker on the squished bag. It says what was inside originally and which squishing method was used, so the other side knows how to unsquish it.

sections.title: Setting Up an IPComp Association
sections.content:
Before using IPComp, two nodes MUST establish an IPComp Association (IPCA). It holds the CPI, the mode of operation, the compression algorithm and any parameters the algorithm needs. The policy can apply to every packet between the nodes or only to selected sessions. Compression can be negotiated in one or both directions, with a different algorithm in each, but an algorithm MUST be chosen for every direction that has an IPCA. There is no default algorithm and none is mandatory.

The CPI value ranges are: 0-63 for well-known algorithms used for manual setup (identical to the IPCOMP Transform identifiers in RFC 2407), 64-255 reserved, 256-61439 negotiated between the nodes, and 61440-65535 for private use. The outbound IPComp header MUST use the CPI chosen by the decompressing node. The CPI together with the destination IP address identifies the compression algorithm characteristics.

The association is set up by dynamic negotiation or manual configuration. Where IPsec is present, dynamic negotiation SHOULD use IKE (RFC 2409). Other protocols MAY be used and are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Before squishing, both sides agree on which squishing method to use. They can talk it over, or an adult can write it on both sides' notes in advance.

sections.title: Negotiating with IKE
sections.content:
With IKE, IPComp can be negotiated stand-alone or together with other IPsec protocols. The initiator sends a Proposal Payload naming the IP Payload Compression Protocol, with one or more Transform Payloads listing the algorithms offered. The CPI travels in the SPI field of the proposal. It SHOULD be sent as a 16-bit number with the SPI size set to 2, or it MAY be sent as a 32-bit value with the SPI size set to 4, in which case the CPI goes in the two least significant octets and the top two octets MUST be zero and ignored. A receiver MUST handle both forms.

Two attributes apply. Encapsulation Mode defaults to Transport Mode, so a proposal that wants Tunnel Mode MUST include the attribute. Lifetime uses the Life Duration and Life Type attributes. An IPComp proposal SHOULD NOT carry attributes meant for other protocols, but it MUST NOT be rejected for lacking them, and any it does carry MUST be ignored.

Two implementation notes follow. A node can offer a CPI in the well-known range, equal to the algorithm's transform identifier, to skip a lookup during decompression. To keep associations unique when several sessions use the same algorithm, CPIs SHOULD come from the negotiated range.
sections.plainLanguage: The two sides pass notes with a number on them that stands for their chosen squishing method. They can write the number in a short or a long box, and both must be able to read either kind.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
When IPComp is used with IPsec, it is believed not to affect the underlying security functionality, and compression is not known to degrade the security architecture or the encryption used.

Without IPsec, payload compression can potentially reduce the security of the Internet, similar to IP encapsulation (RFC 2003). The original Protocol field value and any transport header fields such as port numbers are no longer in their normal places or original values, so a border router can filter the datagram only if it shares the IPCA used for the compression. Allowing this where all packets must be filtered needs a way to securely tell the border router about the association.
sections.plainLanguage: If the contents are squished, the security guard at the gate cannot read the labels. He can only check them if he knows the squishing method.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 2393
sections.content:
This RFC obsoletes RFC 2393. All the changes clarify negotiating an IPCA with IKE in an IPsec context.

  • IPComp can be negotiated stand-alone or bundled with other protocols in a Protection Suite.
  • The CPI in the IKE SPI field is a two-octet field (SHOULD) or four-octet field (MAY), and a receiver MUST process both.
  • The default Encapsulation Mode is Transport Mode, and a proposal for another mode MUST include the attribute.
  • The Lifetime attribute was added to the supported list.
  • Attributes that do not apply to IPComp SHOULD NOT be included and MUST be ignored; a proposal must never be rejected for omitting other transforms' attributes.
  • Implementation notes were added on using well-known CPIs.

The RFC says it requires no IANA actions; the well-known numbers are defined in RFC 2407.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the second edition of the rules. It mostly makes the note-passing between the two sides clearer.

fields.name: Next Header
fields.desc: Original IPv4 Protocol or IPv6 Next Header value.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Reserved; MUST be zero and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Compression Parameter Index
fields.desc: Identifies the compression algorithm, in network order.

items.label: Well-known
items.desc: Algorithms needing no extra information; used for manual setup.

items.label: Negotiated
items.desc: Chosen between the two nodes when defining an IPCA.
